procedural_history.originating_court: Additional District and Sessions Judge, Hosur
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 31st March 2022, passed by the High Court of Judicature at Madras in Criminal Appeal No. 34 of 2019.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The accused No. 1 (appellant in the Supreme Court) appealed the judgment and order of conviction dated 20th December 2018, passed by the Additional District and Sessions Judge, Hosur in S. C. No. 7 of 2007, for offenses punishable under Sections 302 and 341 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The High Court dismissed the appeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (accused No. 1) approached the Supreme Court challenging the High Court's judgment and order dated 31st March 2022, in Criminal Appeal No. 34 of 2019. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

decision.conviction_status: quashed and set aside; acquitted of all the charges
directions: The appellant herein is directed to be set at liberty forthwith, if not required in any other case.

issue.issue_text: Concurrent conviction of the appellant-accused No.1 for oﬀ ences punishable u/ss.302, 341 IPC primarily on the basis of evidence of PW-1, an interested witness, if justiﬁ ed.

facts: The appellant (accused No. 1) was convicted for murder (s.302 IPC) and wrongful restraint (s.341 IPC) by the trial court, and this conviction was upheld by the High Court.
The conviction was primarily based on the testimony of a single witness, PW-1, who was the brother of the deceased.
The Court identified PW-1 as an 'interested witness' due to his relationship with the deceased and an admitted pre-existing enmity between the parties.
Based on the very same evidence from PW-1, the trial court had acquitted ten other accused, and the High Court had acquitted co-accused No. 3.
The High Court distinguished the appellant's case from the acquitted co-accused No. 3 on the grounds that the appellant had absconded and surrendered later.
law: The evidence of an interested witness must be scrutinized with caution.
Previous enmity is a 'double-edged sword'; it can provide a motive for the crime, but it also increases the possibility of false implication.
When a witness's testimony is not found to be wholly reliable or 'above reproach', it requires corroboration in material particulars by other reliable evidence.
A conviction cannot be based solely on the uncorroborated testimony of an interested witness, especially when that same testimony has been disbelieved for other accused in the same case.
application: The Court noted that PW-1's testimony was already found to be unreliable by the lower courts with respect to the majority of the accused, who were acquitted.
Since PW-1's evidence was not considered credible enough to convict others, the Court determined that his testimony fell into the category that requires corroboration.
The Court found the High Court's reason for treating the appellant differently from the acquitted co-accused No. 3 to be 'totally perfunctory'.
As there was no other corroborating evidence to support PW-1's testimony against the appellant, the Court found it unsafe to uphold the conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the conviction could not be justified as it was based solely on the uncorroborated testimony of an interested witness (PW-1), whose evidence had been largely disbelieved by the lower courts. The Court, therefore, quashed the conviction and acquitted the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Evidence – Interested witness – Previous enmity – Conviction based solely on the testimony of interested witness, without corroboration of such testimony – Legality:

facts: The appellant (accused No. 1) was convicted for murder and wrongful restraint.
The conviction was based primarily on the testimony of a single witness, PW-1, who was the brother of the deceased.
There was a pre-existing enmity between the parties, with an ongoing trial related to a prior incident.
The trial court and the High Court had already disbelieved PW-1's testimony with respect to other co-accused, acquitting them based on the very same evidence.
law: The testimony of a single witness can be sufficient for conviction, but only if it is found to be 'above reproach or suspicion of interestedness'.
When a witness's testimony is not wholly reliable, the court must be circumspect and look for corroboration in material particulars from other reliable evidence.
Previous enmity is a 'double-edged sword'; it can establish a motive for the crime, but it also increases the possibility of false implication by the witness.
application: The Court categorized PW-1 as an interested witness due to his relationship with the deceased and the existing enmity.

The Court found PW-1's testimony to be unreliable. The primary reason for this was that both the trial court and the High Court had already acquitted several other accused persons by disbelieving PW-1's testimony against them.
The Court reasoned that if PW-1's testimony was not credible enough to convict the other accused, it could not be considered safe to convict the appellant based solely on that same testimony.
Given the unreliability of the witness and the lack of any corroborating evidence, the Court determined that the testimony fell into the category that requires corroboration.
The High Court's reasoning for treating the appellant's case differently from the acquitted co-accused was found to be 'totally perfunctory'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a conviction cannot be legally sustained when it is based solely on the uncorroborated testimony of an interested witness with prior enmity, especially when that same testimony has been found unreliable by lower courts in the case of other co-accused. The Court therefore quashed the conviction and acquitted the appellant.

arguments.issue_text: Concurrent conviction of the appellant-accused No.1 for oﬀ ences punishable u/ss.302, 341 IPC primarily on the basis of evidence of PW-1, an interested witness, if justiﬁ ed.
appellant_arguments: The High Court grossly erred in convicting the appellant for offences under Sections 302 and 341 of the IPC.
The conviction is based on the evidence of a single witness, PW-1 (Narayanappa).
Another accused (No. 3 – Sridhar Reddy) was acquitted based on the very same evidence from PW-1.
Therefore, the conviction of the appellant on the basis of the same evidence is not tenable in law.
respondent_arguments: The trial court and the High Court concurrently found the appellant guilty based on a proper appreciation of evidence.
No perversity can be found in the concurrent findings of fact by the lower courts.

arguments.issue_text: Evidence – Interested witness – Previous enmity – Conviction based solely on the testimony of interested witness, without corroboration of such testimony – Legality:
appellant_arguments: The conviction is legally untenable as it is based on the testimony of a single interested witness, PW-1.

The unreliability of this testimony is evident because another co-accused was acquitted on the basis of the same witness's evidence, showing a lack of sufficient corroboration to sustain a conviction.
respondent_arguments: The concurrent findings of guilt by the lower courts were based on a proper appreciation of the evidence, including the testimony of the witness, and these findings are not perverse.

cases.case_name: Vadivelu Thevar vs. State of Madras
cases.principle: It is a sound and well-established rule of law that the court is concerned with the quality and not with the quantity of the evidence necessary for proving or disproving a fact. Oral testimony may be classified into three categories for assessment.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is a sound and well-established rule of law that the court is concerned with the quality and not with the quantity of the evidence necessary for proving or disproving a fact.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court's reasoning for distinguishing the case of the appellant from that of the acquitted co-accused (No. 3) was 'totally perfunctory.' When a conviction is based on the testimony of a single witness whose evidence was deemed insufficient to convict a co-accused, the conviction of the appellant on the basis of that same evidence is not legally tenable, as it indicates the witness falls into a category requiring corroboration that was not met.
legal_tests_applied: In line with Vadivelu Thevar vs. State of Madras, when a witness is not wholly reliable or wholly unreliable, the court must be circumspect and look for corroboration in material particulars by reliable testimony, direct or circumstantial, before basing a conviction on such evidence.
policy_considerations: The court must apply evidence consistently to all co-accused. It is unjust to convict one accused while acquitting another based on the exact same testimony from a single witness without a substantial and well-reasoned distinction.
